summary.title: Metal-Free Photocatalysis at Charged Aqueous Interface: Boosting the Photocatalytic Oxidative Coupling of Arylamines to Azoaromatics under Ambient Conditions
summary.authors: Shivendra Singh; Vidhi Agarwal; Tridib K Sarma; Tushar Kanti Mukherjee
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic method for synthesizing azoaromatics from arylamines in water under ambient air. This micellar environment enables non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps, significantly boosting reaction kinetics. The optimized protocol achieves 100% conversion and selectivity within 4 hours using only 0.6 mole% catalyst, outperforming previous methods that required organic solvents, inert atmospheres, or higher catalyst doses. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic method for synthesizing azoaromatics from arylamines in water under ambient air. The authors utilize Eosin Y (EY) as a photocatalyst and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) to form charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs). This micellar environment enables non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps, significantly boosting reaction kinetics. The optimized protocol achieves 100% conversion and selectivity within 4 hours using only 0.6 mole% catalyst, outperforming previous methods that required organic solvents, inert atmospheres, or higher catalyst doses. The mechanism involves atmospheric oxygen acting as a sacrificial oxidant to regenerate the catalyst via hydrogen peroxide formation. This work demonstrates that interfacial charge modulation can overcome solubility limitations and kinetic barriers, offering a green alternative for azo compound synthesis.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are vital for optical storage and molecular switches. Traditional diazotization produces unstable intermediates and waste. Metal-catalyzed methods suffer from slow kinetics and poor selectivity. Photocatalytic reductive coupling requires inert atmospheres. Prior organic photocatalysis uses organic solvents due to solubility. Charged aqueous interfaces modulate reactions via confinement and fields.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can azoaromatics be synthesized in water under ambient air? Do charged interfaces enhance photocatalytic efficiency? Can non-diffusive PET occur at micellar surfaces? Will micelles allow high yields with low catalyst loading? Does the micellar environment overcome solubility barriers?

Methodological Details
The study used Eosin Y as the photocatalyst. CTAB was selected for its positive charge compatibility. Arylamines were the substrates for oxidative coupling. The reaction occurred in water at ambient air. K3PO4 served as the base for proton abstraction. Green light at 525 nm triggered the reaction. Conversion was monitored via GC-MS measurements. Micelle formation was confirmed by HR-TEM. Fluorescence spectroscopy probed PET kinetics. Radical traps validated the amine radical mechanism.

Procedures And Architectures
EY binds to CTAB micelles via electrostatic attraction. Micellization shifts EY absorption by 9 nm. EY fluorescence increases 2.4-fold in CTAB micelles. The Stern layer entraps EY near the CMC. Fluorescence lifetime increases from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns. K3PO4 does not disrupt the EY-CTAB complex. Arylamines solubilize at the hydrocarbon/aqueous interface. PET occurs with a time constant of 0.3 ps. Atmospheric O2 regenerates the catalyst via H2O2. BHT trapping confirmed radical intermediates.

Key Results
100% conversion was achieved in 4 hours. The reaction required only 0.6 mole% catalyst. Selectivity reached 100% for all tested substrates. Electron-rich amines showed 100% conversion. Aniline also achieved 100% conversion. Chloro- and bromo-anilines showed 98% and 95% yields. Previous methods required 64% yield after 24 hours. The catalyst dose was reduced 8.3-fold. The quenching rate constant was 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. H2O2 formation was confirmed by color change strips.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The micellar surface acts as an efficient scaffold. Non-diffusive PET drives the reaction speed. Redox potentials are modulated at the interface. The approach outperforms all previous methodologies. This is the first report on aqueous phase synthesis. The method opens new opportunities for azoaromatics.

Contradictions And Limitations
SDS showed no interaction with EY. TX-100 composite disassembled with K3PO4. p-Nitroaniline did not undergo PET. DABCO base gave slightly lower yields. Blue light required 6 hours for full conversion. BHT trapping reduced yield to ~5%.

Claims
Charged aqueous interfaces enable efficient metal-free photocatalysis for azo synthesis. 100% conversion achieved in 4 hours. Ultrafast PET time constant of 0.3 ps. Low catalyst loading of 0.6 mol%. SDS micelles failed to support the reaction. Electron-deficient substrates like p-nitroaniline failed. Green synthesis in water is now feasible. Interfacial engineering boosts catalytic efficacy.
Non-diffusive PET is the key mechanism for reaction acceleration. Quenching rate constant is extremely high. PET precedes proton abstraction. Radical traps significantly inhibited the reaction. Sub-nanosecond kinetics enable rapid synthesis. Diffusion limitations are overcome by confinement.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Base is essential for proton abstraction. Light wavelength affects reaction time. Micelle type dictates catalyst stability.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows absorption and fluorescence spectra. Figure 2 displays Stern-Volmer plots and kinetics. Table 1 lists optimized reaction conditions.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a metal-free aqueous synthesis of azoaromatics. 2. The strongest evidence is the 100% yield in 4 hours with 0.6 mol% catalyst. 3. The future path involves expanding substrate scope and mechanism studies.
